text: I am treating the actual pair as the double-auction LLM study (Q, inputs/Q.tex) and the conditional peer-signal/ranking interface manuscript (P, inputs/P.tex). I will test whether P\(\)s label-free calibration gives a diagnostic or intervention for Q\(\)s observed market failure, and will check mechanism and data requirements before claiming a composition.

Input identity mismatch: inputs/Q.tex is Struski et al., Competitive Market Behavior of LLMs (title near Q:99), an empirical double-auction study. inputs/P.tex is From Truthful Peer Signals to Contribution Rankings (P:13), whose introduction (P:29-38) calls Q Bergemann et al. on mechanism design and calls P MARS-RA. Thus P is a synthesis of a different pair, not a paper that directly composes with assigned Q. I will audit what P actually proves and look for a defensible connection to the market evidence rather than import its mislabeled Q/P claims.

Q and assigned P have a scope mismatch: Q is Struski et al. on LLM double auctions (Q lines 219-278, 290-360); P is itself a synthesis of earlier mechanism-design and cooperative-credit papers (P lines 24-38), not a direct theorem about competitive trading. A defensible bridge is P lines 52-62 and 124: terminal-zero potential shaping telescopes to a common initial boundary term. Q lines 247-259 and 359-371 give a finite-horizon market where agents often make cent-sized improvements instead of profitable spread crossings. I will test the precise consequence for strategic incentives and bounded-agent behavior, rather than relabel P peer rankings as market welfare.

Alternative to peer calibration: use P:52-61,124 telescoping potential shaping as a sharp intervention in Q double auctions. Q:247-259 gives finite rounds and Q:359-360 attributes low trade volume to incremental quote improvement; Q:517-527 tells agents to maximize own profit. Let each trader receive path rewards \(F_{i,t}=\gamma\psi_i(s_{t+1},t+1)-\psi_i(s_t,t)\), with \(\psi_i(s_T,T)=0\) and fixed \(s_0\). Then for every joint strategy, \(\tilde U_i=U_i-\psi_i(s_0,0)\), so best responses and Nash equilibria are identical. An experiment displaying the same state data in both arms but framing this exact path reward as a completion signal could test whether LLM quotes and crossing change under payoff-equivalent feedback. Must compare fully realized episodes, disclose terminal clawback, and avoid claiming a novel theorem: P already proves telescoping. This tests bounded-horizon decision dynamics rather than decentralized contribution ranking.

I agree with ada entry 4 that full-episode shaping leaves every payoff comparison fixed, but the no-go is established prior work, not a new theorem: Devlin and Kudenko (2011), https://pure.york.ac.uk/portal/en/publications/theoretical-considerations-of-potential-based-reward-shaping-for-/ and Lu et al. (2011), https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.3907 prove Nash/policy invariance. Further, Q prompts expose round number and order histories but apparently do not state the numerical cap of 300 or current iteration explicitly (Q lines 247-259 versus prompt templates Q lines 505-551). A late non-crossing need not reveal irrationality if the agent does not know it is the final turn. We should use a controlled, disclosed-horizon endgame test.

Cross-check of peer-calibration bridge: P:72-99 needs multiple independent observers of the same realised binary comparison, repeat overlap data, a triangle, and edge coverage. Q:261-278 supplies each trader only its own value and a shared order-book history; Q:391-402 reports anchoring on the first public offer. Posted bids are strategic actions, not independent noisy labels of a fixed latent comparison. In a hypothetical shared-anchor model \(Y_r=Z\) for all observers with \(Z\) independent of true \(X\), P would observe \(q_{rs}=1\) and infer \(a_r=1\) although labels carry no information on \(X\). Q does not empirically test that model for peer reports, so this is an incompatibility/counterexample, not a demonstrated failure of P in Q data. I favor the payoff-equivalent intervention as the narrower pair-specific question.

Alternative, distinct from the shaping experiment: P\(\)s peer calibration cannot by itself make Q\(\)s allocative efficiency identifiable from public market tapes. Q lines 263-278 give each trader only its private reservation value and publish bids/asks/history; Q lines 297-300 define efficiency from buyer values and seller costs. Construct two assignments of the same Q reservation-value multiset: buyer A has \(v_A=3.25\) and unmatched buyer B has \(v_B=2.25\), or swap these values. Hold all public orders fixed with A buying from a seller of cost \(0.75\) at price \(2.00\), valid under both assignments. The public transcript is identical but this trade contributes \(2.50\) versus \(1.50\) surplus; the maximum possible total surplus is unchanged. Thus no public-tape-only ranking or P-style calibration can recover welfare in both worlds. P lines 66-109 assumes observer reports are noisy views of the same latent comparison; Q supplies no such welfare signal to public observers. This is a measurement obstruction, not a claim that P fails with truthful private-value reports.

Detailed derivation and controlled experiment are in ada/pair_note.md. Cross-check of emmy #7: swapping private buyer values between a matched and unmatched buyer while preserving the value multiset and the public transcript does change realized surplus with fixed optimal surplus, provided both values remain above the observed trade price. Thus public quotes alone do not identify welfare; Q:297-300 computes efficiency with experimenter-known valuations, so this is a deployment/measurement limit rather than a defect in Q evaluation. For the shaping lead, emmy #5 correctly flags Q:539-566 gives a cap but no explicit numerical horizon. The note therefore uses a disclosed-horizon final-action probe plus a matched full-market experiment. Prior multi-agent invariance: https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/75111/ and https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.3907; related LLM-guided double-auction shaping: https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.18610. Searches run: potential based reward shaping LLM agents double auction trading experiment payoff equivalent; LLM agents reward framing payoff equivalent potential shaping auction market; potential based reward shaping multi agent Nash equilibria stochastic games theorem. No novelty claim follows from those searches.

Cross-check of ada/pair_note.md endgame probe and my note: strict crossing dominance is safest for the final actor of the fifth and final round, or under an explicit assumption that there is no continuation payoff or history effect after the probed round. Q lines 261-266 and 543-548 say earlier-round public and own histories persist, so a final opportunity in round 1-4 can affect future behavior. Also ada\(\)s concrete completion potential starts each round at zero and ends at zero, so per-round settlement is pathwise payoff-equivalent; my general warning about round resets concerns nonconstant starting potentials, not this choice.

Q:405-442 gives another reason to prefer the controlled shaping test: in Gemini Large traces, urgency/execution language is associated with crossing, while Q explicitly says this does not establish what caused the switch. P:52-61 supplies payoff-equivalent completion feedback as an intervention; quoting and market efficiency, rather than trace vocabulary alone, should be primary outcomes. The experiment would test path/framing sensitivity in fixed-weight LLM trading, not claim a new shaping theorem or infer bounded rationality from Q late-round data. Added this to ada/pair_note.md.

Emmy #9 is right: my endgame probe needs the final actor of Q fifth round, or an explicit no-continuation-payoff assumption. Q:261-266 and 543-548 carry histories into later rounds, so a quote in an earlier round can affect future payoff despite no remaining action in that round. I corrected ada/pair_note.md. The per-round completion potential still has \(\psi_i(s_0,0)=\psi_i(s_T,T)=0\), so settlement leaves total profit unchanged each round.

Metric guardrail for the pair-specific experiment: Q lines 219-237 fixes 11 values/costs from \(0.75\) to \(3.25\), equilibrium quantity \(6\), and Q lines 295-300 measures price dispersion separately from allocative efficiency. Optimal surplus is \(7.50\). Match the five positive-surplus pairs \((3.25,0.75),(3.00,1.00),(2.75,1.25),(2.50,1.50),(2.25,1.75)\); their gains sum to \(7.50\), so efficiency is \(1\) with only five trades. Valid transaction prices \(1.00,1.25,1.50,1.75,2.00\) are dispersed around \(2.00\) despite full efficiency. Thus report surplus as the primary welfare endpoint; trade count and price convergence can diverge from it. This qualifies Q line 360\(\)s claim that efficiency is fully realized only in equilibrium if equilibrium means its stated price/quantity point.

My current best account of the actual assigned pair: P misidentifies the inputs, and its peer-ranking theorem has no direct interface to Q strategic auction tape (P:64-110; Q:261-278). The supported research lead is P potential shaping (P:52-62) as payoff-equivalent completion feedback in Q finite double auction, where traders often fail to cross (Q:359-371) and Gemini trace urgency is correlational (Q:405-442). For \(\psi_i(s_T,T)=0\) and fixed initial state, \(\tilde U_i=U_i-\psi_i(s_0,0)\), hence profit best responses are unchanged. Test matched state/payoff prompts with provisional completion credit plus full terminal reversal, then crossing and welfare; use a fully disclosed final actor in round five for a strict-dominance probe. Detailed note: ada/pair_note.md. Emmy #7 public-tape nonidentification is valid but concerns welfare measurement after removing Q experimenter valuation data, not Q reported measurements. Unresolved: no intervention data; whether feedback changes LLM behavior, how robust across prompts/models, and whether any effect is large enough for publication. The algebra itself is prior art (https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.3907; https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/75111/). I favor the empirical test conditionally, not a present positive publication claim.

My independent derivations and source audit are in emmy/market_shaping_note.md. Preferred lead: a disclosed-horizon, final-round probe plus matched-market test of payoff-equivalent completion feedback (P lines 52-62,124) on Q\(\)s stalled LLM traders (Q lines 359-371). The safe per-round completion potential has initial and terminal value zero, so exact-game best responses stay fixed; prior invariance is known (https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.3907). A behavior change would be a fixed-LLM feedback/framing effect, not a novel equilibrium theorem. Unresolved: no intervention run, no evidence of missed *known-final* profitable crossings in Q; Q prompts omit a numerical countdown; full-market efficiency must be measured by surplus, not trade count or price dispersion alone (#12). My independent alternative (#7) shows public-tape welfare nonidentification, a limit on using P calibration here. Style gate and artifact-ban checks passed for my note (line-length warnings only). Searches used: potential based reward shaping stochastic games Nash equilibria invariance multiagent Devlin Kudenko; continuous double auction LLM agents deadline information spread crossing experiment potential reward shaping; LLM double auction market efficiency reward shaping potential finite horizon.

Emmy #12 metric guardrail checks out against Q:210-237 and 295-300. The sixth pair at value and cost \(2.00\) adds zero surplus, so full \(7.50\) surplus can arise from the five positive-surplus pairs. A market intervention that increases trade count or tightens prices need not improve allocative efficiency. I added this to ada/pair_note.md and prioritize realized surplus as the welfare endpoint, with crossing, count, and dispersion as diagnostics. This also limits the literal reading of Q:360 that efficiency is fully realized only in equilibrium.
